newsitem.title: UK: Worldwide Advertising & Media Digest - May 20.
newsitem.headline: Worldwide Advertising & Media Digest - May 20.

text.p: ....REUTERS WORLDWIDE ADVERTISING & MEDIA DIGEST.....
Reuters news from around the world on Advertising, Marketing, Media, the Internet, Brand-name Products and Consumer Trends
ADVERTISING & MARKETING:

NEW YORK - American Express Co. says 21-year-old golf sensation Tiger Woods will be a worldwide spokesman for the financial services company. Terms for the multi-year agreement have not been disclosed but reports are putting the fee as high as $30 million for five years to feature Woods in advertisements for various American Express products, including its financial services and its credit cards.

LONDON - Britain's new Labour government announces it is banning sponsorship of sporting events by tobacco companies, dealing a blow to many of the nation's favourite fixtures. Cigarette companies spend millions sponsoring sports such as cricket, golf, darts, rugby league, show-jumping and Formula One motor racing.

PARIS - Publicis says its turnover rose six percent to 5.18 billion francs ($905.4 million) in the first quarter of 1997, largely due to expansion abroad. Publicis says it has won advertising accounts from Hermes, Vedior, Puiforcat, Arcopal, Galeries Lafayette and Tefal in France, the Spanish national lottery, Spanish Railways and the Spanish Parliament's institutional communication, Swiss telecommunications, Canada's Seagram, and the Mexican yoghurt industry since the beginning of the year.

NEW YORK - McDonald's Corp plans to increase advertising for its 55-cent sandwich specials to clarify the promotion and to try to beef up sales, the Wall Street Journal says. The Journal in its electronic edition says the restaurant chain told franchisees that new in-store signs and counter cards are being shipped to clarify the special pricing.

LONDON - Advertising executives argue that recent controversy in Britain over so-called "alcopops" has more to do with the way the fruit-flavoured alcoholic drinks are packaged than how they were advertised. The Labour government said earlier it would study problems caused by alcopops, amid growing concern they helped cause drunkenness and crime among teenagers.

NEW YORK - Interpublic Group of Cos Inc says it has acquired Advantage International in Washington, D.C., and a majority stake in The API Group of Companies, based in London. Both privately-held companies are sports marketing firms and will form the basis of a new sports marketing group within Interpublic, says the company, with initial billings of around $550 million annually and revenue in excess of $50 million.
LONDON - Britons are growing more tolerant of advertising that refers to sex, death and drugs but bad language and violence are still taboo, Grey advertising agency says.
MEDIA & THE INTERNET:

FRANKFURT - So-called "Business TV", television programming produced by companies to train, inform and motivate employees, is catching on in Germany. Companies that use Business TV say they want to also reach partners and customers with it and cut travel costs. (Reuter)

LONDON - Media owners and marketers need to adapt to the changing marketplace afforded by the Internet, with a greater focus on customising products, Marjorie Scardino, chief executive of Pearson Plc, tells annual meeting of Britain's Advertising Association.

BONN - Deutsche Telekom AG says it plans to increase the fees it charges TV companies for use of its cable network and will meet main customer representatives in Bonn. Telekom says it wants to increase earnings in its cable business and that both private and public channels will be affected by the price increases.

NEW YORK - The New York Times Co says April and year-to-date ad volumes at the New York Times and Boston Globe newspapers are up from 1996 while volume at its Regional Newspaper Group remains flat. April advertising inches at the Times rose 4.1 percent to 406,300 inches. April volume at the Globe rose 3.3 percent to 297,500 inches, while volume at the Regional group was down 0.5 percent to 1.5 million inches.

NEW YORK - Home Shopping Network Inc has agreed to buy a 50 percent stake in Ticketmaster Group Inc, the New York Times says. The Times quotes unnamed sources close to the talks as saying Home Shopping Network is acquiring 47.5 percent of the stake now held by Paul Allen, a co-founder of Microsoft Corp, for $210 million of its stock. Home Shopping Network is the largest home shopping company in the U.S.

CANNES - Cannes festival-goers wonder aloud why the film festival's 50th edition was made up of so many uninspiring films reeking of violence and evil. The jury rescued the jamboree with awards for a quirky Japanese film, "The Eel" by Shohei Imamura, and by flagging its support for two directors who have tussled with censors. (Reuter)

NEW YORK - Flush with cash from the sale of its cable television business last year, E.W. Scripps Co. says it has agreed to pay up to $775 million to buy six daily newspapers and a top-rated TV station to beef up its core operations. Scripps will pay Harte-Hanks Communications Inc. up to $605 million in stock in a deal meant to be tax free, but it has agreed to pay $775 million in cash to Harte-Hanks if tax-free treatment was not feasible.

SYDNEY - Australian Provincial Newspapers Ltd says it has been given the licence to publish PC Magazine in Australia from the title owner U.S.-based computer magazine publisher Ziff-Davis Inc. APN says its magazine publishing unit APN Computing Group planned a period of co-branding with its leading publication, Windows Sources Australia.

LOS ANGELES - Media magnate Rupert Murdoch, who lives in Beverly Hills for two-thirds of the year, is worth an estimated $3.2 billion, making him the richest person in southern California, a business publication reports.
BRAND-NAME PRODUCTS & MARKETS:

NEW YORK - American coffee drinkers are getting a jolt from higher coffee prices on the supermarket shelf but industry analysts say the extra cost is not spurring many to give up their morning cup of java. "Consumers are not yet complaining about the price of coffee," says Donald Schoenholt, president of Gilles Coffee, a Brooklyn, N.Y.-based roaster. "But I believe that's going to change."

MANILA - Officials of the world's big computer and electronic companies say developing Asia-Pacific countries could easily adapt to the fast-changing landscape of the information technology sector. Charles Wang, chairman of Computer Associates International Inc, tells Asian businesspeople that countries in the region had a tremendous thirst and need for new technology that would compel them to enhance existing computer applications to serve local companies.

STUTTGART - Daimler-Benz AG says it plans to grow an average of eight percent per year until 1999, boosting company turnover during this time period to nearly 135 billion marks, reports the employee magazine "Headline". (Reuter)

SYDNEY - Burns Philp & Co Ltd says it will sell its herb and spice businesses in North America and Europe and return its focus to producing yeast. Businesses put up for sale include Tone Brothers, Durkee-French, Spice Islands, British Pepper & Spice, Euroma and Ostmann.

BEIJING - Eridania Beghin-Say SA of France and the Jifa Group of China's northeastern Jilin province have begun construction of a plant capable of processing 300,000 tonnes of corn per year, company officials say. The project, expected to be operational in 1999, will mainly produce starch, glucose and other products, he said.

NEW YORK - Procter & Gamble unit Folgers Coffee Co. says it will raise the list price on its standard 13-ounce can of ground regular and ground decaffeinated coffees by 30 cents due to higher prices of green coffee on the world's futures markets. The increase, which is to take effect immediately, brings the price for a standard can of regular coffee to $3.36, and decaffeinated ground Folgers up to $4.06.
CONSUMER TRENDS:

SHANGHAI - Hong Kong's property developers, having already created one of the most impressive skylines in Asia, are helping to remodel Shanghai at a breathless pace. Most of the British colony's chief developers have at least two or three major building projects around Shanghai, China's largest city, with the focus on creating top-grade office buildings. But the Shanghai property market is facing serious over-supply with no end in sight for the building boom, leaving developers to scramble for tenants.

HONG KONG - Hoteliers say there are rooms galore in Hong Kong for travellers keen to witness the territory's reversion to Chinese rule, despite predictions that all hotel rooms would be reserved months in advance. Britain hands back its colony of more than 150 years to China at midnight on June 30.

GENEVA - A Swiss buyer paid 16,100 Swiss francs ($11,300) for a box of 25 Cuban cigars rarely available commercially, tripling the pre-sale estimate and setting a record price for a cigar at auction, Christie's says. The 25 "Trinidad" cigars, 19 cm (7.5 inches) long each and packed in their original cedar box, were from the special selection of the Cuban national factory generally reserved for diplomats and other dignitaries.
